items.prompt: Kavango Tiles sold 1 800 000 floor tiles last year at N$26 each. Total sales of floor tiles in the region it supplies came to N$78 000 000 over the same year. Calculate its revenue and its market share.
items.canonical_answer:
Revenue = selling price per unit x quantity sold = 1 800 000 x N$26 = N$46 800 000 for the year.

Market share = the business's sales / total sales in the market, over the same period: N$46 800 000 / N$78 000 000 = 0.60, which is 60% of that regional market.

Holding 60% of the tiles sold in its region tells Kavango Tiles that more than half of every tile bought there is one of its own, so its future sales depend more on whether the region builds than on taking work from rivals.
marking_guidance: Formula: revenue = price per unit x quantity sold, and market share = own sales / total market sales.
Substitution must be shown, not only the answer.
Units: N$ on every money figure and a percentage on the share.
Interpretation: one sentence on what a 60% share means for where further sales would have to come from.

items.prompt: Erongo Cranes employs 18 people, has capital employed of N$42 000 000 and revenue of N$30 000 000. Tsumeb Scaffolding employs 90 people, has capital employed of N$6 000 000 and revenue of N$24 000 000. Calculate how many times larger one business is than the other on each of those three measures.
items.canonical_answer:
Employees: 90 / 18 = 5. Tsumeb Scaffolding employs five times as many people.

Capital employed: N$42 000 000 / N$6 000 000 = 7. Erongo Cranes has seven times the capital employed.

Revenue: N$30 000 000 / N$24 000 000 = 1.25. Erongo Cranes has revenue 1.25 times as large.

The ratios point in opposite directions because the two businesses turn different resources into output: Erongo has money in machines and few people to run them, Tsumeb has people and little equipment. Naming either one as 'the larger business' requires saying which measure is being used.
marking_guidance: Formula: each comparison is one business's figure divided by the other's on the same measure.
Substitution must be shown for all three measures.
Units: N$ on the money measures, a count of people on the employee measure, and each ratio expressed as 'times larger'.
Interpretation: the answer must say what it means that the measures disagree, not only report the three ratios.

items.prompt: A regional council is told that Otjiwa Welding employs 90 people with capital employed of N$6 000 000, while Namib Quarry Plant employs 18 people with capital employed of N$42 000 000. For the council the comparison is employees, and Otjiwa Welding is five times the size on it: 90 people drawing wages in the district against 18. items.canonical_answer: They count different things. Number of employees counts the labour the business uses; capital employed counts the value of the long-term funds invested in it. items.prompt: Analyse how a rise in a business's revenue over five years can overstate how much the business has actually grown.
items.canonical_answer:
Start from the condition that revenue is price multiplied by quantity, and that it is recorded in the money of the year in which it arose. If prices in the industry have risen over the five years, then the later revenue figure is counted in money of lower purchasing power than the earlier one. The mechanism is that a rise in the price component alone raises revenue without a single extra unit being sold, so the measured increase mixes two different things - more activity, and dearer money.

The consequence is a size comparison that is wrong in a known direction: it overstates growth whenever prices have risen, and by more the longer the period. A business planning capacity on that figure may order equipment for volume it does not have, and an owner judging performance may credit a sales team for a movement it did not cause. The correction is to compare quantities sold, or to restate the revenue of each year in the prices of one year, before the figure is used for a decision about the size of the business.
marking_guidance: Condition: revenue is price x quantity, recorded in the money of the year it arose.
Mechanism: a higher price raises revenue because the price component rises, with no extra units sold.
Consequence: the measured growth overstates the real increase in activity, by more over a longer period.
The chain must reach a decision the business takes on that figure - capacity planning or judging performance - and say what would correct it.

items.prompt: Swakop Fresh supplies washed salad to hotels along the coast. Its owner tells a supplier that the business 'has 45% of the market'. Explain what the supplier should establish before relying on that figure.

Defined as all fresh produce sold to all customers in Namibia, the same sales would be a very small percentage.

items.canonical_answer: A market share figure moves with how widely the market is defined, and the definition is chosen rather than given. The consequence is that share is a strong measure of competitive position inside one clearly defined market and a weak measure of size in general.

items.prompt: Analyse how the loss of one large customer can move a small business from profit to loss.
items.canonical_answer:
Start from the condition that the business's sales are concentrated: one customer provides a large share of revenue, say 40%. When that customer stops buying, 40% of revenue goes at once. The mechanism is that the business's commitments do not fall in step with its sales: rent is fixed by an agreement, insurance is paid for the year, and salaried staff are on notice periods, so in the weeks after the loss the business is carrying close to its former costs on 60% of its former revenue.

The measurable consequence is that the gap between what comes in and what goes out closes and can reverse, turning a monthly profit into a monthly loss without anything having gone wrong in the work itself. That reaches survival rather than only profit, because losses have to be funded from cash the business may not have. How far the chain runs depends on what the business can change and how quickly - work it can win to replace the customer, premises it can give up, staff it can redeploy - and on whether it holds enough cash to trade through the period while it does so.
marking_guidance: Condition: the starting point is concentration - one customer providing a large share of revenue.
Mechanism: revenue falls at once because the commitments do not fall with it.
Consequence: monthly profit becomes a monthly loss, and the answer must say why the two do not move together.
The chain must reach the survival of the business, and must state what would limit the damage - replacement work, reduced commitments, or cash held.

items.prompt: A furniture workshop in Ongwediva employs six people and makes pieces to order. It has been offered a contract that would require it to double its workforce and standardise its range. Evaluate whether it should stay small.
items.canonical_answer:
It should stay small unless it can serve the contract without giving up the made-to-order work, and the decisive criterion is what its customers are paying for. Its present customers buy from it because each piece is made to a specification they chose and dealt with directly by the maker. Standardising the range is not a change in scale but a change in product: it moves the workshop into a market where buyers compare on price, and in that market a workshop of twelve people buying timber in small quantities is the expensive producer rather than the responsive one.

The strongest argument the other way is real. A single contract that doubles output spreads the workshop's premises and machinery costs over far more pieces, lowers the cost of each one, and gives the owner a predictable order book instead of a stream of individual commissions. If the workshop can run the contract as a separate standard line while keeping the bespoke work, it gains both.

The judgement therefore rests on capacity and on the owner's objective. Where the workshop has the space and the supervision to run two kinds of work, taking the contract is right. Where doubling means the owner stops making and starts managing, and the bespoke customers lose the person they were buying from, the contract buys volume at the price of the business's only real advantage. It reverses if the contract is long enough, and large enough, to make the workshop a low-cost producer in its own right.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a plain recommendation is required, not a list of both sides.
Context: the argument must be made for this workshop - six staff, made-to-order pieces, a contract requiring standardisation.
Criterion: the decisive factor is what the existing customers are buying and whether the two kinds of work can be run together.
Counterargument: must give the real case for taking the contract - cost per piece and a predictable order book.
Condition: must name what would change the judgement - available capacity, the owner's objective, or a contract large enough to change the workshop's cost position.

items.prompt: Analyse how an unplanned succession can damage a family business.
items.canonical_answer:
Start from the condition that much of what makes a founder-run business work is held personally rather than written down: which customers pay late, which supplier will take a rush order, what a vaguely specified job should be priced at. Where a handover happens without an overlap - a sudden retirement, an illness - the successor inherits the premises, the stock and the equipment, but not that knowledge.

The mechanism is that the decisions which depended on it are now made without it. Quotations go out too low on complicated work and too high on simple work; a supplier who used to squeeze in an urgent delivery is not asked in the way that used to work; a long-standing customer, uncertain about the change, tries a competitor and finds the service acceptable.

The consequence is measurable: orders lost, margins squeezed on the work that is won, and revenue falling at the moment the business is also carrying the cost and distraction of the handover. That reaches the survival of the business where its cash reserves are thin. The chain runs this far only where the succession is unplanned; an overlap in which the successor works alongside the founder, with prices and supplier terms written down, breaks it at the first step.
marking_guidance: Condition: the starting point is knowledge held personally and a handover with no overlap.
Mechanism: decisions that depended on that knowledge are now made without it, with named examples.
Consequence: lost orders and falling revenue, and the answer must say why the timing makes it worse.
The chain must reach the survival of the business, and must state the condition that breaks it - a planned overlap and documented knowledge.

items.prompt: Gobabis Hardware is owned by a family and has been managed by the founder for thirty years. Her daughter has ten years' experience running a larger builders' merchant elsewhere; her son has worked in the shop since school and expects the manager's post. Explain the problem the family faces.

The daughter brings experience of running a larger operation of the same kind, which is what the business would need if it is to grow; the son brings ten years of the shop's own customers, suppliers and pricing, which is the knowledge that would otherwise be lost at the handover. Choosing on capability alone risks losing the son and what he knows; choosing on expectation alone puts the business under a manager who has not run one.

items.prompt: A family business that has grown to 80 employees is considering appointing a chief executive from outside the family for the first time. Evaluate whether it should do so.
items.canonical_answer:
It should, and the decisive criterion is the gap between the skills a business of 80 people needs and the pool the family can draw on. Running a business of that size requires managing managers, formal reporting and financial control, and a family of a handful of adults is unlikely to contain someone trained in all of it. Appointing from outside widens the field to the best available candidate and gives capable employees a reason to stay, because the senior posts are open to them as well.

The argument against is not sentiment. What the family supplies - the long time horizon, the willingness to accept a thin year, the reputation attached to the family name - comes from owners who expect to hand the business on, and an outside chief executive judged on annual results has different incentives. If the appointment is made without the family retaining ownership and a board seat, the business may gain management and lose the thing that distinguished it.

So the judgement is conditional on how the appointment is framed: outside management with the family keeping ownership and a defined governance role captures both, and that is the arrangement to recommend. It would change if the family genuinely contains a candidate of the right calibre, or if the business is small enough that the owner-manager can still see all of it, in which case the cost and disruption of the appointment buy very little.

The consequence is that the cost of the training falls on the small workshop while part of the benefit reaches whichever business employs the worker next - it acquires a trained welder without the years of supervision. items.prompt: A settlement of 2 000 people lies 300 km from the nearest city. It has a general dealer, a welding workshop, a taxi operator and two shebeens, all owner-run. Explain what these businesses provide that a large national firm would not.

They provide the services at all. A settlement of 2 000 people does not generate the sales a national chain needs to cover a branch, a delivery route 300 km long and a share of head-office cost, so a large firm would not open there. The owner-run dealer can, because the owner's own labour is the main cost and there is no head office to support.

They also provide the part of the service that depends on knowing the customers: credit until payday for people the dealer knows, a welding repair to a specification nobody wrote down, a taxi run timed around the school. items.prompt: A private limited company running four hardware branches in Namibia can either open three more branches over four years or buy a competitor that already has three. Evaluate whether it should grow organically.

It should grow organically, and the decisive criterion is that it already knows how to run this format. Opening its own branches means repeating something the business has done four times: the layout, the supplier terms, the staff training and the stock list transfer straight across, and the cost is spread over four years so it can be funded from retained profit and borrowing as the business generates them. Buying the competitor puts three branches into the business in one step, but they arrive with somebody else's leases, stock, staff contracts and reputation, and every one of those has to be examined before the price is agreed and reconciled with its own afterwards.

The argument for buying is strong where time matters. If a rival is also expanding, four years of building branches may leave the best sites taken, and the competitor's three branches come with customers already walking through the door rather than having to be won. Organic growth also carries its own risk: three new branches funded from cash flow can outrun the cash, and a business that opens a branch a year is committing before it knows whether the last one works.

On balance organic growth is the right choice for a business of four branches with no urgent competitive threat, because it keeps control of the format and lets each opening be judged before the next is committed. It reverses if the sites are genuinely scarce, if the competitor is available at a price below what three new branches would cost to build, or if the company lacks the management depth to open and run three new branches while running the four it has.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between conglomerate diversification and horizontal integration.
items.canonical_answer:
They differ in how closely the two businesses are related. Horizontal integration combines two businesses at the same stage of the same industry, so the combined business does more of one thing: it gains market share, can remove duplicated functions and faces one competitor fewer. Conglomerate diversification combines businesses in unrelated markets, so the combined business does two different things and gains no duplication to remove and no extra share of either market.

The consequence is that they pursue opposite objectives. Horizontal integration concentrates the business's exposure in one market in exchange for strength in it; conglomerate diversification spreads exposure across markets in exchange for having no particular strength in either.

By putting the business into markets that do not move together. items.prompt: Explain the difference between a friendly merger and a hostile takeover.
items.canonical_answer:
The difference is whether the target's board agrees. In a friendly merger both boards negotiate the terms and recommend the combination to their shareholders, so the two businesses combine by agreement. In a hostile takeover the bidder makes its offer directly to the target's shareholders after the target's board has advised them to refuse it, so control changes hands against the wishes of the people running the business.

The consequence is practical rather than presentational. An agreed bidder is normally given access to the target's records before the price is settled and keeps the managers who know the business; a hostile bidder works from published information and may lose the people it needs once it has won.

items.prompt: Analyse how a business that wins a contested takeover can end up with less than it paid for.

Start from the condition that the bid was opposed: the buyer was not given access to the target's records, so it priced the business from published information, and it raised its offer to overcome the board's advice to refuse. The mechanism has two parts. First, what was not examined can only be discovered after the purchase - contracts on poor terms, equipment near the end of its life, a dispute not yet settled - and each of those reduces the value of what was bought below the price paid for it. Second, the people who know the business have just been told by their own board that the buyer should be resisted, so the managers, the specialists and the salespeople with the customer relationships may leave in the months after the bid succeeds.

The consequence is measurable: the buyer holds a business worth less than it paid, earning less than the forecast that justified the price, while the premium it paid still has to be recovered from the profits of both businesses. The chain is weaker where the target's value lies in premises, equipment and contracts that stay whoever leaves, and strongest where it lies in people and relationships that can walk out.

items.prompt: Evaluate whether the shareholders of a business making a takeover gain from it.

Usually less than the shareholders on the other side, and often not at all, and the decisive criterion is the premium. The buyer pays more than the market price of the target's shares - that is what persuades holders to sell - so on the day the deal completes the buyer's shareholders have exchanged cash or shares for a business at above its quoted value. They gain only if the combined business earns enough more than the two would have earned apart to cover that premium and the cost of combining them, and that improvement has to be delivered afterwards by the same management that has just committed the money.

The case the other way is that the premium buys something real. Where the buyer genuinely can remove duplicated functions, or secure an input it was exposed on, or reach customers it had no route to, the additional earnings are not speculative and the shareholders end up owning a stronger business than they held before.

So the judgement is that buying shareholders gain where the specific improvement was identified and costed before the price was set, and lose where the premium was paid against an expectation of savings that was assumed. What settles it is not the merits of the target but the price: the same business at a lower price would be a gain, and at a high enough price no business is. The judgement reverses where the buyer has acquired something it can measure - a named contract, a removable head office - rather than a general hope of being larger.

Criterion: the decisive factor is the premium paid against the improvement actually available.

The savings were to come from running one function where there were two - one accounts department, one purchasing team, one set of records. The argument against relying on it is that the buyer pays the premium at once and receives the saving, if at all, years later, and that a cheaper route to the same objective often exists - raising output from the plant it already owns, renegotiating its own supply terms, or removing duplication inside its own operations first. Where the saving is an expectation rather than a schedule, the objective is better pursued internally. items.prompt: Evaluate whether a business entering a foreign market for the first time should do so through a strategic alliance rather than by taking over a business already in that market.
items.canonical_answer:
It should start with the alliance, and the decisive criterion is how much the business knows about the market it is entering. A first entry is the point of greatest ignorance: the entrant does not know which customers pay, what the regulations require in practice, or what a business there is worth. Buying outright commits the whole outlay on exactly those judgements. An alliance commits far less, can be ended when the agreement runs out, and returns information - what sells, at what price, to whom - that would make a later purchase a far better-judged one.

The case for buying is real where speed and control decide the outcome. An alliance gives no control over how the product is sold and shares the profit, and the partner acquires the entrant's product knowledge and may later compete with it. If the market is being taken quickly by rivals, the years spent learning through a partner are years in which the positions worth having are filled.

So the recommendation is an alliance first, with the option to buy examined once the market is understood - treating the alliance as a way of pricing the purchase rather than as an alternative to it. It changes where the entrant already knows the market well, where a suitable business is available now and might not be later, or where the product can be copied easily enough that handing it to a partner is the larger risk.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a plain recommendation is required, not a balanced comparison.
Context: the argument must be made for a first entry into a market the business does not know.
Criterion: the decisive factor is how much the entrant knows about the market before committing.
Counterargument: must give the real case for buying - speed, control, and the knowledge handed to a partner.
Condition: must name what would change the recommendation - existing knowledge of the market, a business available only now, or a product easily copied.

items.prompt: A regional development agency is comparing two businesses. Rundu Poultry employs 310 people, has revenue of N$96 000 000 and capital employed of N$24 000 000. Okahandja Feeds employs 62 people, has revenue of N$120 000 000 and capital employed of N$150 000 000. Total sales of poultry feed in the region come to N$400 000 000 a year, of which Okahandja Feeds accounts for N$120 000 000. Calculate the ratio of the two businesses on employees, revenue and capital employed, and Okahandja's market share; then evaluate which measure the agency should use if its purpose is to decide which business does more for the regional economy.
items.canonical_answer:
Employees: 310 / 62 = 5. Rundu Poultry employs five times as many people.

Revenue: N$120 000 000 / N$96 000 000 = 1.25. Okahandja Feeds has revenue 1.25 times as large.

Capital employed: N$150 000 000 / N$24 000 000 = 6.25. Okahandja Feeds has more than six times the capital employed.

Okahandja's market share: N$120 000 000 / N$400 000 000 = 0.30, so it holds 30% of regional feed sales.

Judgement: the agency should use the employee count, with capital employed reported beside it. Its stated purpose is what each business does for the regional economy, and the most direct channel from a business to a regional economy is wages paid to people living in it. On that measure Rundu Poultry is five times the size, and the gap is wide enough that no reasonable weighting of the other measures reverses it.

The strongest argument against is that capital employed measures what has been committed to the region for the long term, and N$150 000 000 of plant is not easily moved elsewhere, whereas employment can be reduced in a bad year. There is also a case for the 30% market share, which shows Okahandja's position in the regional feed market - but a share of one market says nothing about the other business, which is not in it, so it cannot be used to compare the two at all.

The condition is the agency's own purpose. If it is allocating support to sustain employment now, the headcount decides; if it is judging which business anchors long-term investment in the region, capital employed does. What the agency should not do is take a single measure as 'the size' of either business and compare them on it without saying which question it is answering.

If one large employer is deciding whether to stay, the 87.5 jobs at risk in an average large firm could outweigh the diffuse benefit of the centre.

The condition is therefore whether any of the 24 has a decision pending that the site would affect. If none has, the council should fund the centre, because 316 businesses cannot each solve the same problem alone and the smaller firms are also where most new employment in the town will start. items.prompt: Namib Leather tans hides and makes bags. It buys hides from one abattoir, which supplies three tanneries and has raised its price twice in a year, and it sells through 40 independent shops, four of which take half its output. It can buy either a share of the abattoir or the four shops. Analyse the circumstances in which each purchase would suit it, and evaluate which it should pursue.
items.canonical_answer:
Buying into the abattoir is backward integration. It would suit Namib Leather where the binding problem is the input: one supplier, three buyers competing for its hides, and two price rises in a year. Ownership would secure the supply and the terms on which hides transfer, and keep the abattoir's margin on those hides inside the business. It suits only where Namib uses a large enough share of the abattoir's output to justify the outlay; a tannery taking a small fraction of what the abattoir kills buys capacity it cannot use and a business it does not know how to run.

Buying the four shops is forward integration. It would suit Namib where the binding problem is the route to the customer - shelf space at risk, or no sight of what sells. The four take half of output, so the position secured is substantial, and the retail margin on half the output would come inside the business. It suits only where the remaining 36 independents can be kept: they now buy from a competitor, and if a material number reduce their orders, the volume lost from the other half of output can exceed the margin gained on the first half.

Recommendation: pursue the abattoir. The decisive factor is which problem is actually costing money now. Two price rises in a year on a sole-source input, with three tanneries bidding for it, is a live and recurring cost, while the shops are selling the bags without complaint. The strongest argument against is that tanning and slaughtering are different trades and Namib would be buying into a business it has not run - which is why a share, with a supply agreement attached, is preferable to buying the abattoir outright.

The recommendation changes if the four shops signal that they will take another maker's bags, because half of output would then be at risk at once, which outweighs a price rise on hides. It would also change if Namib's share of the abattoir's throughput is too small for a stake to give it any influence over price.
marking_guidance: Both purchases must be analysed before a recommendation is reached.
Judgement: a recommendation is required.

Criterion: the decisive factor must be which problem is currently costing the business money.
Counterargument: must address that the abattoir is an unfamiliar trade, and the risk to the other 36 shops.
